title: How things work
description: Use everyday motion to see how air and machines work.
author: claude

topic.title: How things work
topic.description: Use everyday motion to see how air and machines work.

concepts.title: Lift
concepts.askLine: A paper plane has no engine. So what keeps it up in the air while it glides?
concepts.hook: A paper glider has no engine, yet its wing can hold it up while air moves past. When it slows, that upward force fades.
concepts.rule: A wing makes lift when air flows past it and is turned down. The air pushes the wing up. Lift must match weight for steady level flight.

claims.text: Lift needs motion between a wing and air.
A wing turns air and gets an upward force; in steady level flight lift balances weight.

items.stem: In a classroom, a paper plane slows down as it flies. What happens to its lift (the upward push)?

options.text: It gets weaker.
options.feedback: Less relative airflow can reduce the wing's upward force, so the glider may sink.

options.text: It stays the same, since the shape is unchanged.
options.feedback: The shape is still there, so that sounds right. Less moving air can mean less lift.

options.text: It grows as the plane slows.
options.feedback: Slower air past the wing tends to cut lift, not raise it. That is why a slowing glider sinks.

items.stem: On a train, Om holds a paper wing inside, then out the window in the wind. When does it get pushed?

options.text: When air flows past it.
options.feedback: The force comes from the wing changing the path of moving air, which pushes back.

options.text: Before the wind reaches it, because of its shape.
options.feedback: The curved shape looks ready to lift. It still needs air to move past it.

options.text: Only when the train stops.
options.feedback: A stopped train means less air rushing past. The push comes when air flows over the wing.

items.stem: A toy glider's weight is 2 newtons (a unit of force). In steady level flight, about how much lift does it need?

options.text: 2 newtons.
options.feedback: In level flight at steady height, upward and downward forces match rather than add.

options.text: 4 newtons.
options.feedback: More lift can sound safer. For steady level flight, upward lift matches the two-newton weight.

options.text: 0 newtons, since gliders float.
options.feedback: Gliders do not float for free. Steady level flight needs about 2 newtons of lift to match the weight.

items.stem: A wing pushes air down. Newton's third law says every push has an equal push back. What pushes back?

options.text: Air pushes the wing up.
options.feedback: Pushing air down and getting pushed up are two halves of the same push between the wing and the air.

options.text: Air pushes the wing only backward.
options.feedback: A wing does meet backward drag. Turning air down also brings an upward push.

options.text: Air pulls the wing down.
options.feedback: Pushing air down brings an equal push back up on the wing. A downward pull would not hold a plane up.

items.stem: A glider slows down in still air. Its weight stays the same. Why does it start to sink?

options.text: Less airflow means less lift.
options.feedback: A slower wing may turn less air downward each second, so lift can fall below weight.

options.text: The wing's shape keeps lift the same at any speed.
options.feedback: The shape stays the same, so this sounds right. Lift also needs moving air.

options.text: Slower air gives more lift by staying longer.
options.feedback: Longer contact can sound like more lift. The slower flow may give less upward push.

items.stem: A paper plane flies level. Lift points up, and weight points ___.

options.text: Down.
options.feedback: Those opposite forces balance if its height and speed are steady in this simple picture.

options.text: Forward.
options.feedback: The plane moves forward, so that direction comes to mind. Weight pulls down.

options.text: Sideways.
options.feedback: Weight always pulls toward the ground. In level flight it points down while lift points up.

items.stem: A model wing lifts in a wind tunnel. Isha expects the same lift at that speed in a vacuum, with no air. What is wrong?

options.text: There is no air to push down.
options.feedback: Matching speed is not enough: the wing needs air to receive an upward push.

options.text: The wing can push on empty space the same way.
options.feedback: Its shape is still there. But no air means no air to turn down.

options.text: Same speed gives same lift, whatever is around it.
options.feedback: The wing keeps its speed and shape. With no air, it has nothing to turn down.

items.stem: Put the steps of wing lift in order.

options.text: Air flows past the moving wing.
options.feedback: Lift needs moving air first. A still wing in still air makes no lift.

options.text: The wing turns that air downward.
options.feedback: The angled wing changes the air's path and sends it down behind the wing.

options.text: The air pushes the wing up.
options.feedback: Turning air down brings an equal push back up, which can balance the weight.

misconceptions.name: Shape alone lifts
misconceptions.correction: A still wing needs moving air to make lift.

misconceptions.name: Air is not pushed
misconceptions.correction: Wings turn air; the air pushes back on them.

quest.title: Try a paper wing
quest.detail: Fold a paper glider. Watch what happens as it slows. Mark the air flow and the lift path on a sketch.

concepts.title: How a multirotor turns
concepts.hook: A quadcopter can spin in place while its four rotors stay flat. It does this by changing how hard each pair of rotors twists.
concepts.rule: A multirotor changes motor speeds to shift thrust. Uneven thrust tilts it in pitch or roll; a change in the spin force balance turns it in yaw.

claims.text: A gap in motor speeds can make a drone pitch or roll.
Yaw comes from a change in the balance of rotor turning force.

items.stem: At a school drone show, the rotors on one side push harder. What does the drone do?

options.text: Tilts toward the weaker side.
options.feedback: Unequal upward push makes a turning effect on the craft before it moves sideways.

options.text: Stays level, since all rotors still run.
options.feedback: All rotors are on, so it can seem balanced. One side now pushes harder and tips the craft.

options.text: Climbs straight up with no tilt.
options.feedback: A straight climb needs every rotor to push harder together. One stronger side tips the craft instead.

items.stem: In a college lab, a hovering four-rotor drone turns its nose. What changed?

options.text: The balance of the rotors' spin.
options.feedback: Yaw comes from uneven turning moments, even while total upward thrust can still hold height.

options.text: The GPS changed its target, not the rotor forces.
options.feedback: A position command can guide the controller, but a physical turn needs a change in rotor forces.

options.text: The propellers were swapped mid-air.
options.feedback: Nothing is swapped in flight. The controller changes motor speeds, which shifts the spin balance and turns the nose.

items.stem: To tip a drone nose down, its two rear rotors push 2.5 newtons each. Total thrust stays 8. What does each front rotor push?

options.text: 1.5 newtons.
options.feedback: The stronger rear pair gives five newtons. The front pair must share three to keep total thrust at eight.

options.text: 2.5 newtons.
options.feedback: Matching 2.5 values look balanced. They would leave no front-rear gap to tip the craft.

options.text: 2 newtons.
options.feedback: Leaving the front at 2 would raise total thrust to 9. The front pair must drop to 1.5 each to keep 8.

items.stem: A drone tips its nose down. What simple cause fits?

options.text: The rear rotors push more than the front.
options.feedback: The rear side lifts more, rotating the body toward a lower nose.

options.text: All rotors push equally all the time.
options.feedback: Equal thrust can hold a hover. To pitch down, the rear must push harder.

options.text: The GPS points the nose down.
options.feedback: GPS can guide where the craft goes, but motor speeds make the tilt. More rear thrust lowers the nose.

items.stem: A four-rotor drone hovers with equal thrust. Why do its rotors still spin in opposite directions?

options.text: Opposite spins cancel the twist on the body.
options.feedback: Even when each rotor lifts equally, its spin can turn the craft. Opposite spins help balance that turn.

options.text: Opposite spins matter only when moving forward.
options.feedback: A hover looks still. The rotors can still twist the craft unless spin effects balance.

options.text: Equal thrust already cancels every twist.
options.feedback: Equal upward push looks fully balanced. Rotor spin can still twist the craft around.

items.stem: Roll tilts a drone side to side. Yaw turns it around the ___ axis.

options.text: Vertical.
options.feedback: A nose turn in place is yaw, which differs from a side tilt or forward pitch.

options.text: Front-to-back.
options.feedback: The long axis runs through the craft, so it sounds like a turn. It names roll.

options.text: Side-to-side.
options.feedback: The side-to-side axis is the one for pitch, nose up or down. Yaw turns around the up-down axis.

items.stem: GPS shows a drone drifted left, so its controller speeds up some rotors. Ravi says GPS pushed it right. What is wrong?

options.text: The motors made the push.
options.feedback: GPS supplied a position clue; the controller used it to change rotor forces that moved the craft.

options.text: GPS makes the fix once it knows the error.
options.feedback: A good position clue helps the controller. The motors still need to change force.

options.text: The position signal is the push that moves it.
options.feedback: GPS shows the drift, so it can seem to fix it. Motors make the force.

items.stem: Match each drone motion with its force pattern.

options.text: Roll
options.feedback: A lateral imbalance tips the craft around its front-to-back axis.

options.text: Unequal side-to-side thrust
options.feedback: A stronger push on one side can tip the craft about its front-to-back axis.

options.text: Yaw
options.feedback: The nose turns left or right while the body spins about its upright axis.

options.text: Unequal rotor spin moments
options.feedback: The spin forces no longer cancel, so they can twist the craft in place.

misconceptions.name: GPS steers motors
misconceptions.correction: GPS can aid position, but speed changes at motors make the turn.

misconceptions.name: All speeds same for turn
misconceptions.correction: A turn needs a change in the balance of motor forces.

sources.title: Mathematical Modeling of Quadcopter Dynamics
sources.publisher: Qikai Huang, Rose-Hulman Institute of Technology

sources.title: VNAV Lab 3: Modelling and control of UAVs

quest.title: Sketch four motors
quest.detail: Draw a top view of a four-motor craft. Mark which side needs more thrust for a roll. Label yaw, pitch, and roll.

concepts.title: Batteries and flight time
concepts.hook: Doubling a drone battery does not double flight time. The bigger battery is heavier, so the motors work harder.
concepts.rule: Flight time rests on usable battery energy and how fast the motors spend it. A larger battery adds energy and weight, so time need not rise in step with size.

claims.text: Flight time depends on stored energy and the rate at which it is used.
A heavy battery adds weight, so the craft needs more lift.

items.stem: A school drone gets a heavier battery with more energy. What happens to its flight time?

options.text: It rises, but less than the energy did.
options.feedback: The extra mass raises the force and power needed to stay aloft.

options.text: It rises as much as the energy did.
options.feedback: Twice the stored energy suggests twice the time. Extra battery mass may raise power use.

options.text: It falls below the old time.
options.feedback: More energy can still add some time. The extra weight eats into the gain, but need not wipe it out.

items.stem: At a hostel robotics meet, a drone carries a heavy camera. What changes when it hovers?

options.text: The motors must give more lift.
options.feedback: The extra load adds weight, so the rotors must supply more upward force.

options.text: Hover power stays the same; rotor count did not change.
options.feedback: The same rotors still fly, which makes this seem reasonable. Carrying more weight can make them use more power.

options.text: The rotors need less lift now.
options.feedback: Extra load adds weight, so the rotors must push harder, not less. Hover power tends to rise.

items.stem: A heavier 180 watt-hour battery makes a drone hover at 90 watts instead of 60. About how many hours can it fly?

options.text: 2 hours.
options.feedback: The larger battery stores more energy, but its added weight makes the motors use power faster.

options.text: 3 hours.
options.feedback: The old 60-watt rate is easy to reuse. The heavier pack raises power use to 90 watts.

options.text: 1 hour.
options.feedback: Energy over power gives 180 divided by 90, which is 2 hours. One hour would need a 180-watt draw.

items.stem: Two batteries hold the same energy, but one is heavier. In the same drone, which gives a shorter flight?

options.text: The heavier battery.
options.feedback: It asks the motors to support more mass while providing no extra stored energy.

options.text: The lighter one, which uses more power.
options.feedback: The lighter pack stores less, so it may seem less useful. It needs less lift in hover.

options.text: Both the same, since energy is equal.
options.feedback: Equal energy is only half the story. The heavier pack needs more lift, so it spends that energy faster.

items.stem: A bigger battery holds more energy, yet the drone gains little flight time. How can both be true?

options.text: The extra weight raises hover power.
options.feedback: Extra energy helps, but the motors may spend it faster while lifting the heavier craft.

options.text: Battery weight cannot change hover power.
options.feedback: The larger pack brings more energy. Its extra mass also asks the motors for more work.

options.text: More energy gives the same percent more time.
options.feedback: More energy often means more time. Extra mass can also make the motors work harder.

items.stem: Flight time is stored energy divided by how fast the drone uses it. What is that rate called?

options.text: Power use.
options.feedback: A craft that spends energy faster drains the same store in less time.

options.text: Rotor count alone.
options.feedback: Rotor count is easy to see. It does not tell how fast the craft uses stored energy.

options.text: Battery weight.
options.feedback: Weight changes how much power the craft needs, but the rate in the sum is the power use itself.

items.stem: A heavier battery holds twice the energy. Tara predicts exactly twice the flight time. What could break that?

options.text: The added weight raises power use.
options.feedback: The larger energy store can drain faster because the rotors must carry more mass.

options.text: Extra weight matters at takeoff, not in hover.
options.feedback: Takeoff may feel like the hard part. A heavier craft also needs more lift while it hovers.

options.text: Battery energy alone sets flight time.
options.feedback: The battery rating looks like the full answer. Power use also sets how fast it runs down.

items.stem: Why are flight-time charts only estimates?

options.text: Usable energy and power use both change.
options.feedback: Wind, payload, and battery mass affect how fast the stored energy is spent.

options.text: The battery rating fixes flight time, whatever the power use.
options.feedback: Stored energy is an important input, but the craft's power use can change with weight and flight conditions.

options.text: Sellers just make them up.
options.feedback: Charts come from tests under set conditions. Wind and payload change power use once the craft is out flying.

misconceptions.name: Double size, double time
misconceptions.correction: More battery adds weight, so time need not scale with size.

misconceptions.name: Weight costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: More weight needs more lift and motor work.

sources.title: Flying Batteries: In-flight Battery Switching to Increase Multirotor Flight Time
sources.publisher: Jain and Mueller, University of California Berkeley

quest.title: Draw an energy trade
quest.detail: Sketch two made-up batteries. Add arrows for more stored energy and more mass. Say how each may change flight time.

concepts.title: Flight sensors
concepts.hook: A roof can block a drone's map signal. Yet the drone still feels a quick tilt.
concepts.rule: An IMU senses quick motion and turning. GPS helps locate the craft when signals are clear. A barometer reads air pressure to help track height. Each clue can be imperfect.

claims.text: An IMU can sense a fast turn and a change in speed.
GPS can help find a place. A barometer reads air pressure to help track height.

items.stem: In a school lab, a drone under a roof tilts quickly. Which sensor notices the tilt?

options.text: The motion sensor (IMU).
options.feedback: The IMU feels a quick spin or push. It needs no clear view of the sky.

options.text: The pressure sensor, since it senses height.
options.feedback: Height sensing can work under a roof. The quick tilt clue comes from the IMU.

options.text: Only the satellite receiver (GPS).
options.feedback: GPS tracks position, so it sounds like the motion clue. The IMU feels fast tilt nearby.

items.stem: On a train platform under a roof, a drone's map dot wanders. What has weakened?

options.text: The GPS satellite signal.
options.feedback: A roof can block or bounce the signal. The map dot may drift, though tilt sensing works.

options.text: The barometer's sense of height.
options.feedback: Both sensors can help with height, so they are easy to mix up. A wandering map dot under a roof points to a weak GPS signal.

options.text: The IMU's sense of tilt.
options.feedback: The IMU works on board and does not need the sky. A wandering map dot points to weak GPS.

items.stem: Under a roof, weak GPS says 18 metres high. A checked barometer (air-pressure sensor) says 12 metres. Which height should the drone use?

options.text: The 12-metre pressure reading.
options.feedback: The roof weakens GPS here. Air pressure gives a second clue to height.

options.text: The 18-metre weak GPS reading.
options.feedback: GPS can estimate height, but the weak signal under the roof is a reason to check another clue.

options.text: The average, 15 metres.
options.feedback: Averaging mixes in a reading the roof has weakened. The checked pressure reading is the better clue here.

items.stem: Which sensor reads air pressure to track height?

options.text: A barometer.
options.feedback: Air pressure changes with height, though weather and other effects make it an imperfect clue.

options.text: A GPS antenna alone.
options.feedback: GPS can report height, so it seems to fit. But it is the barometer that uses air pressure.

options.text: The IMU.
options.feedback: An IMU senses quick turns and motion, not air pressure. A barometer reads pressure to track height.

items.stem: Under a roof, a drone loses GPS for a moment but keeps flying. Why can it still use its IMU?

options.text: The IMU senses motion between GPS fixes.
options.feedback: The IMU tracks quick turns and moves while the GPS signal is weak. Its errors can grow.

options.text: The IMU stops once GPS drops out.
options.feedback: GPS is a strong map clue. The IMU can still sense quick motion on its own.

options.text: The IMU gives exact map points without satellites.
options.feedback: Fast motion data can seem like a full map. An IMU alone cannot fix an exact spot.

items.stem: An IMU senses a quick spin. A map location is helped by ___.

options.text: Satellite signals.
options.feedback: GPS uses several space signals to find a place. The tilt sensor works on board.

options.text: The barometer alone.
options.feedback: Pressure can help estimate height, but map location needs a position clue such as GPS.

options.text: The motor speed.
options.feedback: How fast motors spin moves the craft but says nothing about where it is. A map spot needs satellite signals.

items.stem: Under a roof, a GPS dot wanders. Dev averages its readings and calls the result exact. What is wrong?

options.text: Blocked signals can still leave it wrong.
options.feedback: A roof can block or bend signals. Taking their average may still leave the dot wrong.

options.text: More readings make a blocked signal exact.
options.feedback: More data can cut random noise. A shared roof error may still remain.

options.text: Averaging removes every roof error.
options.feedback: More readings often help. A roof can skew them all in the same way.

items.stem: A drone flies under a school roof. Which line fits?

options.text: Tilt sensing still works; GPS gets worse.
options.feedback: The IMU feels movement on board. A roof may block the space signals.

options.text: The roof blocks satellites and the tilt sensor.
options.feedback: The roof blocks sky signals, so all sensing may seem gone. The IMU still feels tilt.

options.text: The barometer stops working indoors.
options.feedback: Air pressure reaches under a roof too. The roof mainly harms the satellite signals that GPS needs.

misconceptions.name: GPS senses all turns
misconceptions.correction: The IMU gives quick turn and motion clues.

misconceptions.name: One sensor is perfect
misconceptions.correction: Signals and readings can have limits, so each clue can err.

quest.title: Make a sensor map
quest.detail: On paper, draw a drone and link tilt, place, and height to IMU, GPS, and barometer. Add one limit for each.

concepts.title: Why birds flap but planes do not
concepts.hook: A bird can flap for both lift and forward push; a jet keeps fixed wings while its engine supplies the forward push.
concepts.rule: Bird flaps can help give lift and forward push. A plane’s fixed wings make lift as air moves past them, while an engine or propeller gives forward push.

claims.text: Bird wing flaps can provide lift and thrust.
A plane can use fixed wings for lift and engines or propellers for thrust.

items.stem: From a train, a student sees a bird flapping alongside. What does each wing stroke give it?

options.text: Lift and forward push.
options.feedback: The changing wing motion can push air in ways that support and propel the bird.

options.text: Lift only, no forward push.
options.feedback: Wings are often linked only with lift, but a bird's stroke can also help move it forward.

options.text: Cooling for the bird's body only.
options.feedback: Flapping is not mainly for cooling. Each stroke pushes air to give the bird lift and forward push.

items.stem: On a school trip, a jet passes over. Its wings do not flap. How does it stay up?

options.text: Air flows past its fixed wings.
options.feedback: The engine gives forward motion, and the moving air lets the wings make lift.

options.text: Wing shape lifts even with no air moving.
options.feedback: Its shape is easy to see. The wing still needs moving air to make lift.

options.text: Engine thrust holds it up.
options.feedback: The engine keeps the plane moving, so it can seem to provide all support. Airflow over the fixed wings creates the lift.

items.stem: A plane weighing 500 newtons flies level. Its engine pushes forward with 200 newtons. How much lift must the wings make?

options.text: 500 newtons.
options.feedback: The wings hold up the plane's weight. Engine push acts forward and does not take the place of that lift.

options.text: 200 newtons.
options.feedback: The engine's 200 is the visible force. Lift points up and must match the 500-newton weight.

options.text: 700 newtons.
options.feedback: Adding the two mixes up directions. Lift must match the 500-newton weight on its own.

items.stem: On a plane, what mainly pushes it forward?

options.text: The engine or propeller.
options.feedback: It pushes the craft forward so air can flow over the fixed wings.

options.text: The wing's upward lift.
options.feedback: The wing supplies an important force, but that force is upward; the engine mainly supplies forward thrust.

options.text: The tail fin.
options.feedback: A tail helps steer and keep the plane stable. Forward thrust comes from the engine or propeller.

items.stem: A bird glides without flapping. A plane flies on fixed wings. What lets both wings lift?

options.text: Air must flow past and be turned down.
options.feedback: Either wing can receive an upward push when it deflects moving air.

options.text: Only powered wings make lift.
options.feedback: Flapping can add motion. A gliding wing also meets moving air.

options.text: Both wings must flap to move air.
options.feedback: Birds often flap, so it looks required. A glide also moves air past a wing.

items.stem: A jet engine mainly gives thrust. The fixed wings mainly give ___.

options.text: Lift.
options.feedback: Keeping these roles apart helps explain flight without making the wing flap.

options.text: The engine's main forward thrust.
options.feedback: The engine is loud and visible. It gives thrust while the wings make lift.

options.text: Drag.
options.feedback: Wings do make some drag, but that is a side effect. Their main job is to make lift.

items.stem: A plane's engine stops, but it glides for a while. Sam says only flapping wings lift without an engine. What is missing?

options.text: Gliding keeps air moving past fixed wings.
options.feedback: The plane can trade height for motion, and its fixed wings can still make lift.

options.text: A fixed wing stops lifting when the engine stops.
options.feedback: The engine drives flight, so this feels likely. A glide still keeps air moving past the wing.

options.text: Only the engine can move air past a wing.
options.feedback: The engine drove the plane, so lift may seem to stop with it. A glide keeps air flowing.

items.stem: What do birds and planes share in flight?

options.text: Both use moving air for lift, in different ways.
options.feedback: Bird wingbeats can add thrust, while a plane engine drives air past its fixed wings.

options.text: Both need flapping wings to move air.
options.feedback: Flapping is familiar from birds, but gliding birds and fixed-wing planes can both get lift from moving air without wingbeats.

options.text: Planes flap their wings too, just slowly.
options.feedback: Plane wings stay fixed. Air pushed past them by the engine's thrust is what makes their lift.

misconceptions.name: All wings must flap
misconceptions.correction: A fixed wing can lift when air moves past it.

misconceptions.name: Engine makes all lift
misconceptions.correction: The engine gives forward thrust; the wing makes most lift.

sources.title: Birds Repurpose the Role of Drag and Lift to Take Off and Land

quest.title: Spot two pushes
quest.detail: Watch a bird and a plane clip. Draw an arrow for forward push and one for lift on each.

concepts.title: How a ceiling fan moves air
concepts.hook: A fan can cool sweaty skin in a warm classroom, yet the air stays warm. Where did the cooling happen?
concepts.rule: Angled fan blades push air and make it flow through the room. The breeze can help people feel cooler, but the fan does not make cold air.

claims.text: A ceiling fan moves room air with rotating blades.
A breeze can aid cooling at the skin, but a fan does not make cold air.

items.stem: A classroom fan starts. The window stays shut. What reaches a student's face?

options.text: Room air, moving faster.
options.feedback: The blades push air through the room, giving a breeze without making new cold air.

options.text: Air the fan has cooled.
options.feedback: The breeze feels cooler on skin, which suggests colder air. The fan moves room air rather than lowering its temperature.

options.text: Fresh air from outside.
options.feedback: With the window shut, no outside air comes in. The fan just speeds up the air already in the room.

items.stem: In monsoon heat, a hostel fan runs in an empty room. Who or what does it cool?

options.text: No one, since nobody is there.
options.feedback: The motor still moves air, but the main cooling effect needs a person beneath it.

options.text: The room air itself.
options.feedback: A fan feels cool on skin. In an empty room, it just moves the air.

options.text: People in the next room.
options.feedback: A ceiling fan moves air mainly in its own room. With no one beneath it, nobody feels the breeze.

items.stem: A fan's breeze makes a student feel cool, but no heat leaves the room. By how many degrees does the room air cool?

options.text: 0 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: The fan moves room air over skin. That can cool the student without lowering the air temperature.

options.text: 3 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: A cool feeling on skin is not a three-degree drop in the room air.

options.text: 10 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: A fan has no way to remove ten degrees of heat. It moves air over skin while the room stays as warm.

items.stem: Why does moving air feel cooler on skin?

options.text: It helps sweat dry (evaporate).
options.feedback: Moving air helps sweat dry. That can cool skin while the room air stays warm.

options.text: The fan chills the air before it reaches you.
options.feedback: The breeze feels cool, so the air may seem colder. It helps sweat dry; the room stays warm.

options.text: Moving air holds less heat.
options.feedback: Moving room air holds the same heat as still air. It feels cooler because it helps sweat dry.

items.stem: Fan blades are tilted. Why does the tilt matter?

options.text: It pushes nearby air along as it turns.
options.feedback: The blade pushes air along; that moving air can then pass over skin.

options.text: A flat blade would move air just as well.
options.feedback: The motor makes the motion. Blade tilt helps aim and push the air.

options.text: A blade cools the air mainly by touching it.
options.feedback: A spinning blade touches air, so this sounds right. Its tilt steers the breeze.

items.stem: A fan moves room air. An air conditioner can lower the air's ___.

options.text: Temperature.
options.feedback: The devices can feel similar to a person, but only one removes heat from the room air.

options.text: Speed over your skin.
options.feedback: A breeze feels cool on skin. An air conditioner can cool the air in the room too.

options.text: Noise level.
options.feedback: An air conditioner can be loud or quiet, but its job is to remove heat. It lowers the air's temperature.

items.stem: Under a fan, Meera feels cooler, but the room thermometer has not changed. She says the room is cooler. What did she mix up?

options.text: Cooler skin and cooler room air.
options.feedback: Moving air helps sweat dry and cools skin. The room thermometer can stay the same.

options.text: A breeze turns warm air into cold air.
options.feedback: The moving air may feel cooler, but its temperature need not fall.

options.text: Skin and air must cool by the same amount.
options.feedback: A fan can help skin lose heat without lowering the temperature of all the room air.

items.stem: Which line best explains a fan on a hot exam day?

options.text: Moving air cools skin without chilling the room.
options.feedback: The breeze helps sweat dry, which takes heat from the skin, while the room air stays about as warm.

options.text: A fan cools room air without moving heat out.
options.feedback: The breeze feels cool on skin. The fan moves air without chilling the room.

options.text: A faster fan makes the air colder.
options.feedback: A faster fan moves more air, which can feel cooler. It still does not lower the room's temperature.

misconceptions.name: Fan makes cold air
misconceptions.correction: A fan moves the air already in the room.

misconceptions.name: Spin has no push
misconceptions.correction: Angled spinning blades move air.

sources.title: Energy-Saving Hacks To Beat the Summer Heat

quest.title: Map a breeze
quest.detail: With the fan on, hold a light ribbon safely away from the blades. Sketch which way the air flows.

concepts.title: How UPI moves money
concepts.hook: A UPI ID helps route a payment between bank accounts; the money is not stored in the ID.
concepts.rule: The payer approves a UPI request, NPCI routes it, and the linked banks carry out the transfer.

claims.text: A UPI ID is a payment address linked to a bank account.
UPI transfers money between bank accounts through the NPCI system.

items.stem: At a college canteen, Asha pays to a seller's UPI ID. Where does the money come from?

options.text: Her linked bank account.
options.feedback: The ID points the request to accounts; it is not a separate pot of cash.

options.text: Cash held in the app until the seller accepts.
options.feedback: The app shows the pay screen, so it can look like a wallet. The linked bank sends the funds.

options.text: A balance stored inside the ID.
options.feedback: The ID appears on the pay screen, so it can look like a wallet. The bank holds the funds.

items.stem: On a train, Ravi shares his UPI ID to get a refund. What can the sender do with it?

options.text: Find where to send the money.
options.feedback: The sender can direct money to that ID without being given the full account number.

options.text: See Ravi's private UPI PIN.
options.feedback: The ID helps a sender find Ravi. It does not reveal his private PIN.

options.text: Take money out of Ravi's account.
options.feedback: A UPI ID lets money be sent to Ravi. Money leaves his account only when he approves with his PIN.

items.stem: A student has ₹1,500 in a bank account linked to her UPI app. She deletes the app. How much stays in the bank?

options.text: About ₹1,500 in the bank.
options.feedback: The app is an interface to the linked account. Deleting it does not move the money held by the bank.

options.text: About ₹0 after deleting the app.
options.feedback: The app can show a balance, but the linked bank holds these funds. Removing the app is not a transfer.

options.text: About ₹3,000 as bank and app balances.
options.feedback: The app does not hold a second copy of bank money. The bank still has ₹1,500.

items.stem: In UPI, what is a VPA?

options.text: A virtual payment address, like your UPI ID.
options.feedback: It is an ID used to direct a payment without typing the full account details.

options.text: A balance held by the payment app.
options.feedback: The app displays an ID and a balance, so they can seem to be the same thing. The VPA is an address linked to a bank account.

options.text: A bank branch code.
options.feedback: That is the IFSC, a different code. A VPA is a virtual payment address linked to a bank account.

items.stem: Kiran says a UPI app sends money without any bank. What is wrong?

options.text: UPI moves money between bank accounts.
options.feedback: The app is a front door to a bank-to-bank payment through the shared system.

options.text: The UPI ID holds the cash until it is sent.
options.feedback: The ID appears on screen, so it can look like a wallet. It names a payment address.

options.text: The app's own balance replaces the bank.
options.feedback: The app is the visible part of payment, but linked banks carry out the account transfer.

items.stem: The payer approves, NPCI (India's payment network) routes it, and the linked ___ move the money.

options.text: Banks.
options.feedback: The debit and credit belong to the linked accounts at the banks.

options.text: Payment apps alone.
options.feedback: The apps start and display the transfer, but the linked banks hold the accounts that move the money.

options.text: Phone companies.
options.feedback: The phone network carries the message, but it does not hold the money. The linked banks move the funds.

items.stem: A classmate says a UPI ID alone proves a payment is done. What is missing?

options.text: Approval and a completed transfer.
options.feedback: The UPI ID only says where money should go. The payer still has to approve a payment that then goes through.

options.text: Sharing the ID means the money is paid.
options.feedback: The address is ready to use. A payment still needs approval and a transfer.

options.text: An address is the same as a receipt.
options.feedback: An address looks like payment proof. It only tells where money could be sent.

items.stem: Which line best explains a UPI payment?

options.text: An ID guides a bank-to-bank transfer through NPCI.
options.feedback: The app starts it, the payer approves it, and the system routes it to accounts.

options.text: An ID stores cash until the phone opens.
options.feedback: The ID is visible in the app, so it may look like storage. It points to a bank account.

options.text: NPCI keeps the money and pays later.
options.feedback: NPCI routes the request but does not hold the money. The linked banks debit and credit the accounts.

misconceptions.name: ID is a wallet
misconceptions.correction: The address helps find an account, but it does not itself hold the money.

misconceptions.name: App alone moves cash
misconceptions.correction: The app starts the request while the payment system and banks do the transfer.

quest.title: Trace a payment
quest.detail: In a made-up canteen payment, label the payer, payee, ID and banks.

concepts.title: How a phone camera takes a photo
concepts.hook: A camera lens aims light at a sensor. Millions of tiny light readings are then turned into a photo.
concepts.rule: A phone sensor reads light at tiny sites. The phone then makes a photo from the data.

claims.text: Tiny sites in a phone sensor turn light into a charge.
Red, green and blue filters help the phone make a colour photo.

items.stem: A student takes a phone photo in a dim hostel room. What reaches the sensor through the lens?

options.text: Less light from the scene.
options.feedback: The sensor can only measure the light that enters during the shot.

options.text: A finished picture made by the lens.
options.feedback: The lens frames the scene, so it can seem to paint it. It sends light to the sensor.

options.text: Extra light from the screen.
options.feedback: The screen does not light the scene for the sensor. Only light from the scene comes through the lens.

items.stem: At a college fest, a phone camera faces bright stage lights. What does each tiny sensor spot record?

options.text: How much light hits it.
options.feedback: Each tiny site reads light. The phone then makes the image data.

options.text: A light reading saved by the lens itself.
options.feedback: The lens aims light, so it can seem to record it. The sensor makes the reading.

options.text: A full colour picture of that spot.
options.feedback: A finished photo has colour at each point, but each sensor site first records a light signal for later processing.

items.stem: Phone camera sensors put a red, green or blue filter on each tiny spot. About how much of the filter grid is green?

options.text: About 50%.
options.feedback: A Bayer block has two green sites, one red and one blue. Two out of four is 50%.

options.text: About 33%, one third for each colour.
options.feedback: There are three colours, but the Bayer pattern gives green two of every four sites to capture more detail.

options.text: About 25%, the same as red.
options.feedback: Red has one site in a four-site Bayer block. Green has two sites, or 50%.

items.stem: In a phone camera, what part first turns light into a signal?

options.text: The sensor.
options.feedback: Its tiny light-sensitive sites make signals from the light that arrives.

options.text: The screen glass.
options.feedback: The screen shows photos, so it can seem to make them. The sensor first reads light.

options.text: The lens.
options.feedback: A lens bends light to focus it, but it makes no signal. The sensor turns light into readings.

items.stem: Two phones have the same pixel count but different lenses. Why can their photos differ?

options.text: Different light reaches the sensor.
options.feedback: Pixel count alone says little about the lens or the later image processing.

options.text: The lens matters only if pixel counts differ.
options.feedback: Pixel count is easy to compare. Lens quality can alter the light even at the same count.

options.text: Pixel count makes the lens not matter.
options.feedback: Pixel count is easy to compare. Lens light and later processing can still change the photo.

items.stem: A lens has aimed light at a phone sensor. What step is left before there is a photo?

options.text: Turn the sensor readings into an image.
options.feedback: The sensor records light signals; the phone processes those readings into the final picture.

options.text: Let the lens store a finished image.
options.feedback: The lens guides light but does not store the picture. The sensor readings still need processing.

options.text: Point the lens at the scene again.
options.feedback: The light has already reached the sensor. What is left is to turn its readings into a picture.

items.stem: A classmate says each sensor pixel stores a tiny full-colour painting. What is wrong?

options.text: Each pixel records only a light reading.
options.feedback: Filters sort the light. The phone uses many readings to make a colour photo.

options.text: Each pixel stores a full colour from the scene.
options.feedback: The final photo has colour. Each site first gives a light reading for later work.

options.text: Every pixel holds a finished scene.
options.feedback: The final photo shows a scene, so each site can seem like a tiny copy. It reads light.

items.stem: Which order best explains a phone photo?

options.text: Light, then sensor signals, then processing.
options.feedback: The lens guides light to sites that produce data for a final photo.

options.text: The lens makes a photo; the sensor saves it.
options.feedback: The lens frames the scene, so it can seem to finish the photo. The sensor must read light first.

options.text: Screen, then light, then sensor.
options.feedback: The display only shows the result at the end. Light comes first, then sensor signals, then processing.

misconceptions.name: Pixel is painted ink
misconceptions.correction: A sensor site detects incoming light; the displayed colour is formed from readings.

misconceptions.name: Lens stores the image
misconceptions.correction: The lens directs light, while the sensor records the signal.

sources.title: Technology Originally Developed for Space Missions Now Integral to Everyday Life
Image Sampling with the Bayer Color Filter Array
sources.publisher: Palum, Eastman Kodak Company, IS&T PICS Conference

quest.detail: In a made-up phone diagram, label lens, sensor and saved image.

concepts.title: Blue sky and red sunsets
concepts.hook: Air scatters blue light more than red. At sunset, light takes a long path through the air, so mostly red gets through.
concepts.rule: In clear air, blue light scatters across the sky. Near sunset, a longer air path removes more blue from direct sunlight.

claims.text: Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more easily in Earth’s air than red ones.
At sunset sunlight crosses more atmosphere, so direct light can look red or orange.

items.stem: On a clear Delhi afternoon, which colour of sunlight spreads most across the sky above a school?

options.text: Blue.
options.feedback: Shorter blue wavelengths spread in many directions and reach eyes away from the Sun.

options.text: Red only.
options.feedback: The Sun can look warm red, so red comes to mind. Blue scatters more across clear air.

options.text: Green.
options.feedback: Its waves sit between blue and red. Blue, with the shortest waves here, scatters most across clear air.

items.stem: From a train at sunset, the Sun looks orange near the horizon. What changed about the light's path?

options.text: It passed through more air.
options.feedback: The longer path scatters more blue out of the direct beam.

options.text: The Sun changed its own colour.
options.feedback: The Sun looks new at dusk. Its light has passed through more air on the way.

options.text: Clouds dyed the light orange.
options.feedback: Clouds can add colour but do not dye the light. The longer air path removes more blue from the beam.

items.stem: Scattering goes as 1 ÷ wavelength to the fourth power. About how many times more does blue light (450 nm) scatter than red (700 nm)?

options.text: About six times.
options.feedback: Use (700 ÷ 450) to the fourth power, which is about 5.9. Shorter blue light scatters more strongly.

options.text: About 1.6 times.
options.feedback: That is only the wavelength ratio, 700 ÷ 450. Rayleigh scattering raises this ratio to the fourth power.

options.text: About the same for both colours.
options.feedback: Clear air scatters both, but blue light scatters much more than red light.

items.stem: Blue light scatters more than red in clear air. What about blue light explains this?

options.text: Its shorter wavelength.
options.feedback: In clear air, shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer red light.

options.text: Its longer wavelength.
options.feedback: Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red. That is why it scatters more in clear air.

options.text: Its brighter glow.
options.feedback: Brightness is not what sets scattering here. Blue's shorter wavelength makes it scatter more.

items.stem: Why is a clear sky blue while the low Sun looks red?

options.text: The light reaches you by different paths.
options.feedback: Scattered blue reaches the side view; the long direct path has less blue left.

options.text: Different kinds of sunlight colour the sky and Sun.
options.feedback: The views look unlike. The same light takes different paths through the air.

options.text: The Sun gives off red light only near the horizon.
options.feedback: The low Sun looks red, so its output can seem different. The longer air path scatters more blue from the direct beam.

items.stem: At sunset, sunlight crosses a longer path of ___.

options.text: Air.
options.feedback: That longer route lets more short blue light scatter out of view.

options.text: Only red light from the Sun.
options.feedback: The direct beam looks red at sunset, but it crossed a longer path of air that scattered away more blue light.

options.text: Empty space.
options.feedback: Sunlight crosses space on every trip. At sunset, what grows is the path through air, which strips out blue.

items.stem: Raj says a red sunset proves the Sun sent out no blue light. What is missing?

options.text: The blue scattered away along the path.
options.feedback: The beam began with many colours; air changes which reach the eye directly.

options.text: Blue light vanishes before reaching the air.
options.feedback: The direct beam looks red. Blue light was in it, then spread along the air path.

options.text: The Sun sends less blue light at sunset.
options.feedback: The beam looks red, so the Sun may seem to change. Air scatters more blue along the path.

items.stem: Which line links the blue sky and red sunset?

options.text: Blue spreads sideways; a long path leaves red.
options.feedback: Scattering sends blue around the sky while sunset light loses more blue directly.

options.text: The Sun gives off mostly red light at dusk.
options.feedback: The Sun appears red, but the longer path through air changes which colours remain in the direct beam.

options.text: Dust makes the sky blue by day.
options.feedback: Clear air alone scatters blue light. Dust and haze can change sunsets, but they are not why the sky is blue.

misconceptions.name: Sky is blue paint
misconceptions.correction: The colour comes from scattered sunlight, not dye in the air.

misconceptions.name: Sun turns red
misconceptions.correction: The same Sun is seen through a longer path of air near the horizon.

Aerosols in the Atmosphere
sources.publisher: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies

quest.detail: Draw a short noon path and a longer sunset path through clear air.

concepts.title: Pressure cooker
concepts.hook: A sealed cooker raises pressure, so water can boil at a higher temperature.
concepts.rule: Higher pressure raises water’s boiling point. The hotter water and steam can cook food faster than an open boil.

claims.text: Water boils at more heat when the air above it has more push.
A pressure cooker can cook faster because its hot liquid and steam reach above an open pot’s normal boil.

items.stem: In a family shop kitchen, a sealed pressure cooker heats dal. What happens to the water's boiling point?

options.text: It rises as pressure rises.
options.feedback: With more push on it, the water needs more heat to boil.

options.text: It drops because the lid is heavy.
options.feedback: A heavy lid can look like a cooling weight. Its pressure lets water boil hotter.

options.text: It stays at 100 degrees no matter what.
options.feedback: That is the open-pot boil at sea level. Higher pressure inside lets the water boil hotter.

items.stem: In a hostel kitchen, one pot of beans is open and one is a pressure cooker. Which can boil hotter?

options.text: The pressure cooker.
options.feedback: More push lets the sealed pot boil at a higher heat.

options.text: The open pot, with a bigger flame.
options.feedback: A bigger flame makes more bubbles, so hotter water seems likely. Open pressure stays about the same.

options.text: Both reach the same heat in the end.
options.feedback: Open water stops near its boiling point however long it heats. The sealed pot can boil hotter.

items.stem: At full working pressure, about how hot can the boiling water in a pressure cooker get, in degrees Celsius?

options.text: About 121 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: Georgia State’s example puts the boiling point near 121 degrees at that pressure.

options.text: About 100 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: The open-pot value is easy to recall. Higher pressure can lift the boil near 121 degrees.

options.text: About 150 degrees Celsius.
options.feedback: That is far above the standard example. Georgia State puts the boil near 121 degrees at working pressure.

items.stem: What does higher pressure do to water’s boiling point?

options.text: Raises it.
options.feedback: Water needs more heat before its vapour can form bubbles under greater pressure.

options.text: Lowers it.
options.feedback: More push might sound like less room to heat. Higher pressure raises the boiling point.

options.text: Leaves it unchanged.
options.feedback: Pressure does change the boiling point. With more pressure, water must get hotter before it boils.

items.stem: Both pots hold boiling water. Why does dal cook sooner in the pressure cooker?

options.text: The cooker's boiling water is hotter.
options.feedback: The word boiling does not mean the same temperature at every pressure.

options.text: Only because steam adds flavour.
options.feedback: Steam is easy to notice. Pressure lets the boiling water get hotter.

options.text: A strong flame makes both boils as hot.
options.feedback: Both pots boil, so equal heat seems fair. The cooker has more pressure and a hotter boil.

items.stem: An open pot goes from a high hill down to sea level, where air pressure is higher. Its boiling point goes ___.

options.text: Up.
options.feedback: More pressure at sea level lets water reach a hotter boil than on a high hill.

options.text: Down.
options.feedback: Lower pressure on a high hill lowers the boiling point. More pressure at sea level raises it.

options.text: Nowhere; it stays put.
options.feedback: Air pressure changes with height, so the boiling point shifts too. At sea level it goes up.

items.stem: Sana says a strong flame makes an open pot boil as hot as a cooker. What is wrong?

options.text: Pressure, not flame size, sets the boiling point.
options.feedback: Once the open pot boils, more heat makes more steam. It stays near the same heat.

options.text: More flame raises the open pot's boiling point.
options.feedback: The water boils harder, so it may seem hotter. The open pot keeps the same air pressure.

options.text: Any flame raises the open pot's pressure.
options.feedback: A large flame makes a hard boil. It does not seal the pot or raise its pressure.

items.stem: Which line explains how a pressure cooker works?

options.text: Higher pressure allows a hotter boil.
options.feedback: Hotter water and steam can transfer heat to food faster than an open boil.

options.text: The whistle drives heat into the food.
options.feedback: The whistle marks a pressure change, which can seem to be the cause. Higher pressure lets the water boil hotter; the sound does not heat the dal.

options.text: Less heat escapes, since the steam stays in.
options.feedback: Steam does leave through the whistle. The real gain is the hotter boil that the higher pressure allows.

misconceptions.name: Pressure pushes flavour in
misconceptions.correction: The extra push lets the water boil at a higher heat.

misconceptions.name: More flame raises an open boil
misconceptions.correction: Once open water boils, extra heat mainly makes it boil away faster.
